abstract: This Brookings Institution report analyzes how generative AI technologies will disrupt the American labor market, finding that over 30% of workers could see at least 50% of their occupation's tasks affected by AI. Unlike previous automation technologies that targeted routine blue-collar work, generative AI will primarily disrupt middle- to higher-paid white-collar occupations and clerical roles, with women facing disproportionately high exposure. The authors argue that current policy, employer practices, and worker power are inadequate to manage this transition, and recommend priority action in three areas: establishing responsible employer practices, enhancing worker voice through alternative models beyond traditional unionization, and developing protective public policies.
keyFindings: More than 30% of all U.S. workers could experience at least 50% of their occupation's tasks disrupted by generative AI, while approximately 85% of workers could see at least 10% of their work tasks impacted.

Generative AI will primarily disrupt middle- to higher-paid white-collar occupations in business, finance, law, engineering, and administrative support rather than manual blue-collar work, marking a departure from previous 'skill-biased' automation technologies.

Women face significantly higher exposure to generative AI disruption than men, with 36% of female workers in highly exposed occupations compared to 25% of male workers, particularly in clerical and administrative support roles that employ nearly 19 million Americans.

The industries most exposed to generative AI have some of the lowest union representation in the economy, with unions representing only 1% of finance workers and 6% of private sector workers nationally, creating a critical mismatch between risk and worker bargaining power.

Current U.S. policy, employer practices, and worker organizations lack the urgency, frameworks, and tools needed to manage generative AI's labor market impacts, despite existing examples like the 2023 Hollywood writers' agreement demonstrating effective worker protections.
methodology: Brookings Metro analyzed task-level exposure data from OpenAI relating predicted ChatGPT-4 exposure to thousands of tasks across 1,016 occupations defined by the Department of Labor's O*NET database. OpenAI employed human annotators and GPT-4 itself to assess task exposure, with implied impacts aggregated to the occupational level using a midrange 'exposure' rating statistic. To assess automation feasibility, the authors analyzed OpenAI data estimating the likelihood of ChatGPT-4 completing tasks without human oversight, categorizing tasks with high exposure and high autonomous completion likelihood as 'more likely to automate.' The research was conducted October 2024 and draws on a Brookings workshop convening over 30 experts from policy, business, labor, academia, civil society, and philanthropy.
qualifiers: The authors explicitly note that exposure analyses often overstate potential job impacts by not accounting for practical workplace constraints including legal and business risks, ethical and privacy concerns, and consumer preferences. Task-based analysis may understate impact by missing major technological disruptions not easily captured in task-level approaches (e.g., AI fashion models disrupting the fashion industry). The data does not project future capability enhancements from next-generation models (ChatGPT-5, 6, etc.). The exercise captures only part of the story—it neither accounts for generative AI's impact on job quality as opposed to labor quantity, nor does it capture emergence of new tasks and occupations. Finally, a job's 'exposure' to generative AI does not necessarily predict job loss, as actual outcomes depend on specific employer choices, market responses, and existence of worker protections. The authors characterize their analysis as offering 'a rough-draft speculation' and acknowledge that 'our understanding of the risk to livelihoods is so limited and our national conversation about solutions lags behind the technology.'
